pests.name: Aphids
pests.note_beginner: Tiny green or black soft insects that cluster on new growth and buds, leaving sticky honeydew and curled leaves. Chamomile is otherwise nearly pest-free, and the flowers themselves bring in ladybugs and hoverflies whose young eat aphids. A strong spray of water or insecticidal soap handles a bad patch.
pests.note_seasoned: The one pest chamomile draws with any regularity. Soft-bodied sap-feeders colonize tender tips and buds, secreting honeydew; soft, overfed growth is the most susceptible. Usually held in check by the beneficial predators the flowers recruit, so hose off or treat with insecticidal soap only if populations build, and keep nitrogen low to reduce the lush growth aphids prefer.

pests.name: Thrips
pests.note_beginner: Very slender insects that rasp at flowers and leaves and can leave silvery flecks or distorted blooms, mostly in hot, dry spells. They are a minor issue on chamomile. Keep plants healthy, and a blast of water or insecticidal soap knocks back a heavy patch.
pests.note_seasoned: A minor, occasional pest of the flowers in hot, dry weather, causing stippling and some petal distortion. Rarely damaging enough to treat on a trouble-free herb like chamomile; monitor blooms, and use water sprays or insecticidal soap only if numbers climb. Not specifically documented on the chamomile extension pages, so treated as a general garden-flower pest.

pests.name: Mealybugs
pests.note_beginner: Small, soft, white cottony insects that cluster on stems and leaf joints, mostly on indoor or container plants, leaving sticky honeydew. Uncommon on chamomile outdoors. Dab them off with a cotton swab or treat with insecticidal soap.
pests.note_seasoned: An occasional problem chiefly on container-grown or indoor chamomile, appearing as white, waxy clusters at stem nodes with honeydew and sooty mold. Rare on healthy garden plants; spot-treat with alcohol on a swab or insecticidal soap. Not specifically documented on the chamomile extension pages, so treated as a general container-plant pest.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.note_beginner: A white, powdery film on leaves, most common in crowded plantings and warm, humid, still weather. Chamomile is usually trouble-free, so this shows up mainly when plants are packed together or the air is stagnant. Space plants for airflow, grow in full sun, water at the soil, and remove badly affected growth.
diseases.note_seasoned: The most likely foliar disease on chamomile, favored by crowding, shade, humidity, and overhead wetness, and sharpest as warm, muggy weather sets in. Chamomile is generally disease-free, so cultural control carries it: full sun, generous spacing, base watering, and sanitation. It is worst in the humid heat of a hot-region summer, one reason chamomile is grown in the cooler part of the year there.

diseases.name: Botrytis (gray mold)
diseases.note_beginner: A fuzzy gray mold that rots flowers and stems in cool, damp, crowded conditions, and it can spoil flowers as they dry if they are packed together while still moist. Give plants room for air, water at the base, and dry picked flowers spread out in a single layer.
diseases.note_seasoned: Gray mold, favored by prolonged moisture, dense plantings, and poor airflow, which can blight flowers on the plant and also spoil harvested heads that are piled damp. Manage with spacing, base watering, and prompt, single-layer drying of picked flowers; excess moisture is the driver, so lean, well-drained, airy plantings rarely see it.

diseases.name: Damping-off (seedlings)
diseases.note_beginner: Young seedlings collapse at the soil line and die, caused by cold, wet, poorly drained soil or sowing too thickly. Sow into well-drained soil that is not soggy, do not overwater seedlings, and thin crowded ones so air can move.
diseases.note_seasoned: Seedling collapse from soilborne fungi in cold, wet, poorly drained, or overcrowded conditions, the standing risk when surface-sown chamomile is kept too wet. Prevent rather than treat: well-drained soil, restrained watering, thin stands, and good airflow. Do not sow into cold, waterlogged ground.
